rows.title: Steve Jobs sold his Volkswagen to raise $1,300 for Apple’s first computer. He became a millionaire just two years later at 23
rows.standfirst: Steve Jobs sold his car to raise enough money to build Apple’s first computer. Just one year later, the tech titan reeled in nearly $3 million thanks to that early sacrifice.

rows.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s advice to workers scared of AI: You’re just confusing your job with the tools you use to do it
rows.standfirst: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s advice to workers scared of AI: You’re confusing your job with the tools you use to do it.

rows.title: ‘Inflationary surge’: Fed economists warn AI hype is overheating the economy whether or not the technology ever delivers
rows.standfirst: Economists from the St. Louis Fed said AI could inflate prices today even without a payoff tomorrow.

rows.title: Deutsche Bank asked AI if it’s true that AI will solve the economy’s inflation problems. The robots answered
rows.standfirst: The answer from the machines was unfortunately not what Wall Street wanted to hear.

rows.title: How AI and ‘experience creep’ are making it harder for new graduates to find jobs
rows.standfirst: Recent graduates going into tech face a double bind: Fewer entry-level openings and employers demanding experience that’s nearly impossible to get.

rows.title: Starbucks is offering $1,200 bonuses, expanded tipping, and weekly payouts to boost the pay of its U.S. baristas
rows.standfirst: Starbucks will offer up to $1,200 in bonuses each year and expanded tipping options for its U.S. hourly workers as the company pours $500 million into a turnaround effort.

rows.title: The jobs report looks good ‘for the wrong reasons,’ top economist warns: It’s hiding how many Americans are giving up
rows.standfirst: The strong March number takes rate cuts off the table, and lets the Fed focus squarely on inflation.

rows.title: MIT created duplicate AI workers to tackle thousands of different tasks. The verdict? Most of the time AI is still just ‘minimally sufficient’
rows.standfirst: AI is improving fast, but it has a long way to go before it can outperform humans in demanding tasks.

rows.title: In this buyer’s market, one home seller took an offer $10,000 below asking price, covered $5,000 in closing costs, and paid for $12,000 in repairs
rows.standfirst: “The war in Iran has seriously complicated the spring buying season,” said Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com.

rows.title: Labor market turns upside down as the economy can shed jobs and still keep unemployment low amid immigration reversal
rows.standfirst: “Real-time data point to an important change in the U.S. labor market: The benchmark for evaluating payroll growth has moved significantly.”

rows.title: The founder of a $2.5 million AI-powered legal business started work at her DA’s office at just 12 years old
rows.standfirst: Logan Brown, the founder of AI-powered law firm Soxton, lived out her “Legally Blonde” dreams through hometown court hearings as a preteen and attending Harvard Law School.

rows.title: Meet the Gen Z grads reviving accounting—colleges are reporting near-perfect placement rates at $80K starting salaries
rows.standfirst: Once seen as boring and synonymous with tax season dread, accounting is now attracting Gen Z with high demand, near six-figure salaries, and near-guaranteed job offers.

rows.title: Fortune Archives: Who gets a seat at the table?
rows.standfirst: The pressures were different, but in 1939 as in 2026, unemployment was a thorny problem to solve.

rows.title: Netflix cofounder says he stopped work at 5 p.m. every Tuesday for 30 years to stay ‘sane,’ no matter the crisis: ‘Nothing got in the way of that’
rows.standfirst: Marc Randolph ran Netflix for seven years and never let a meeting, crisis, or last-minute request stand in the way of his Tuesday 5 p.m. hard stop. Experts and fellow CEOs are divided on whether that’s genius—or naive.

rows.title: AI angst mutates into ‘FOBO’ as Fear of Becoming Obsolete takes over American workforces
rows.standfirst: EY’s Joe Depa says he sees a split in staff. There’s “high adoption, right out of the gate” for juniors, but senior workers “are somewhat resistant.”

rows.title: This AI founder is hiring Gen Z with zero experience because they’re not stuck in ‘old ways of working’
rows.standfirst: 38% of bosses plan to hire fewer grads this year. This ex-Google exec is doing the opposite—hiring Gen Z with zero experience or degree required.

rows.title: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon predicts AI will cut the workweek down to 3.5 days—and tells Gen Z developing EQ is more important than ever
rows.standfirst: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon believes that future generations will have more job opportunities, and human skills like curiosity and work ethic will reign supreme in the AI era.

rows.title: AI is cutting 16,000 U.S. jobs a month—and Gen Z is taking the brunt, Goldman Sachs says
rows.standfirst: New research finds younger, entry-level workers bearing the brunt of AI’s labor market disruption—even as the technology creates jobs elsewhere.

rows.title: Anthropic’s research shows that AI can already do a huge portion of many jobs; its top economist talks about how that could shape the future of work
rows.standfirst: Peter McCrory talks about Anthropic’s latest analysis of AI’s role in occupations from computer programming to groundskeeping.

rows.title: Only one in five workers feel like their jobs are safe—manufacturers, warehouse workers, and women are the most worried
rows.standfirst: As AI reshapes work, most employees no longer feel like their jobs are safe—but those in manufacturing, construction, transportation, and warehousing are feeling the least confident.

rows.title: Top economist Mark Zandi says the indicator that has called every recession since WWII just signaled we’re already in one
rows.standfirst: The Vicious Cycle Index is a recession indicator that takes labor force participation changes into consideration. The top economist at Moody’s Analytics said it’s flashing red.

rows.title: Sam Altman and Vinod Khosla agree: AI will break the economy. Their fix is no income tax for most Americans
rows.standfirst: The venture capitalist’s proposal to eliminate income taxes for earners under $100,000 now has a powerful institutional ally—the most valuable AI company on the planet.

rows.title: A Wall Street bank is giving workers earning under $100K over $6,000 in cash to get on the property ladder
rows.standfirst: U.S. staffers at Wall Street bank BNY earning $100,000 or less can qualify for a $6,500 down payment perk to buy their first home, in an effort to support the “financial security and economic prosperity” of its workers.

rows.title: The housing market has been frozen for 3 years. Here’s why this spring could finally change that
rows.standfirst: Affordability is improving, first-time buyers are returning and inventory is slowly rising. Here’s what to watch this season.

rows.title: ‘You can never really catch up’: The Iran war is exacerbating already high grocery bills, and it will only get worse if the war continues, experts say
rows.standfirst: Labor shortages, inflation, and energy costs were raising prices even before the war began, economists say.

rows.title: Trump’s 2027 budget gambles on rosy assumptions—and if they don’t pan out, America edges closer to a fiscal crisis driven by runaway interest costs
rows.standfirst: $7.8 trillion in extra revenue, GDP growing at 3%, vanishing deficits, and a 42% defense hike—to skeptics Trump’s math just isn’t adding up.

rows.title: Gen Z watched millennials burn out at their desk—now 1 in 4 are ditching office jobs for trade jobs
rows.standfirst: Gen Z was sold the dream of white-collar work. Now 75% associate it with instability—they’re ditching desk jobs for drains and electrical cables.

rows.title: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon says he’s ‘learned and relearned’ to not make big decisions when he’s tired on Fridays
rows.standfirst: Over the course of his Wall Street career, JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon has learned to avoid making big decisions when the weekend rolls around.

rows.title: Eva Longoria secretly worked as a headhunter from her soap opera dressing room for three years—because she refused to be a ‘struggling actor’
rows.standfirst: Before an $80 million fortune and Desperate Housewives fame, Eva Longoria was secretly working as a headhunter from her soap opera dressing room for years.

rows.title: The job market is so bad, workers now think they have worse odds of finding a role than during the pandemic
rows.standfirst: Data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York shows that Americans are increasingly pessimistic about their job prospects.

rows.title: ‘Downward mobility is incredibly radicalizing’: The college bargain is broken. What comes next could reshape America
rows.standfirst: “Creative, brilliant people are going to wake up this decade and realize the jobs that they thought they were going to have … are gone.”

rows.title: ‘I thought I was gonna die with it’: ‘The Pitt’ star admits his $80,000 student loan burden nearly made him quit acting and move to a remote Alaskan village
rows.standfirst: Patrick Ball, who plays Dr. Frank Langdon on “The Pitt,” admits he nearly quit acting altogether after struggling to make ends meet, even years after earning two degrees.

rows.title: United Airlines CEO judges candidates by whether pilots would want to go on a four-day trip with them: ‘If you say no, then they’re out’
rows.standfirst: Scott Kirby, the CEO of $31.7 billion company United Airlines, said he looks to hire employees who others would “want to hang out with.”

rows.title: Biggest jump in gas prices in 60 years, biggest jump in inflation since Biden: CPI carnage in March
rows.standfirst: The first read on inflation to capture the effects of the Iran war suggests the budgets of many lower- and middle-income households will be stretched.

rows.title: Inflation goes up by a whopping monthly rate of nearly 1%—and it’s hitting you at the grocery store and gas station
rows.standfirst: Energy was the hardest-hit category, but that didn’t spare consumer goods like coffee.

rows.title: The ‘affordability economy’ has created a housing market nobody predicted: Prices collapsing in the Sunbelt, soaring in the Rust Belt
rows.standfirst: Las Vegas, Austin, and Miami are now leading a national price downturn, while metros like Cleveland, Pittsburgh, and Milwaukee are finally having their moment.

rows.title: The ‘Tuscan Mom’ aesthetic is taking over TikTok as Gen Z glamorize McMansions and reject millennial gray
rows.standfirst: From terracotta walls to wrought-iron fixtures, a new generation is reclaiming the early-2000s interiors their millennial predecessors were desperate to escape.

rows.title: Warren Buffett says ‘accumulating great amounts of money’ doesn’t achieve greatness—He still lives in a $31,500 Nebraska home and clipped coupons
rows.standfirst: Berkshire Hathaway mogul Buffett, worth $143 billion, said kindness is more golden than big bank accounts. He still eats at McDonald’s, and said luxury purchases wouldn’t make him happier.

rows.title: Palantir CEO says AI ‘will destroy’ humanities jobs, but there will be ‘more than enough jobs’ for people with vocational training
rows.standfirst: Alex Karp said he struggled to market his humanities skills to get his first job.

rows.title: These cofounders quit corporate jobs, took on $100K in credit card debt, and slept in a Denny’s—now their $1.2B company is backed by Serena Williams
rows.standfirst: Wemimo Abbey and Samir Goel, the cofounders of fintech company Esusu, quit their corporate jobs and exhausted their savings on the road to unicorn status.

rows.title: Haiti stares down starvation as Iran War drives 200,000 into acute food emergency status
rows.standfirst: Even before the war, about half of Haiti’s 12 million people were in a state of food emergency, according to the UN.

rows.title: Investors are writing off any move from the Fed this month. Collapsing talks in Iran have sealed the deal
rows.standfirst: “It is too soon to identify potential second-round effects in inflation or labor markets,” cautioned UBS’s Paul Donovan.

rows.title: ‘It tastes like a Twinkie’: Major tech podcaster Kara Swisher says AI is overhyped for one simple reason—humans don’t like it
rows.standfirst: Fears about AI’s transformation of the job market may be overblown, according to veteran journalist Kara Swisher—and it’s all thanks to a growing desire for something real.

rows.title: U.S. naval blockade on Iran will trigger a currency devaluation spiral and hyperinflation, potentially ending the war more quickly, analyst says
rows.standfirst: “Leaning on this money machine sends the economy into a tailspin, giving the mullahs much needed motivation to negotiate in earnest.”

rows.title: The most valuable worker in the AI economy is Nurse Dana from ‘The Pitt’
rows.standfirst: Nursing has become the most structurally durable career in America. A hit TV show and a top economist help explain why.

rows.title: Most of Wall Street points to high oil prices as the driver of inflation. A maverick Johns Hopkins economist says they’re chasing the wrong culprit
rows.standfirst: The oil crisis will end with the war; it’s the inflation predicament that has legs, predicts Steve Hanke of Johns Hopkins.

rows.title: He was coding at 12 like Elon Musk and became one of Google’s youngest-ever CMOs—but now says Gen Z is better off ice skating than learning to code
rows.standfirst: Like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, Alon Chen coded his way to success. Now, he says, AI has made the skill “obsolete” for Gen Z.

rows.title: ‘I don’t need help’: Meet some of the AI resisters who smell their own extinction
rows.standfirst: Scott Segal, a 53-year-old social worker, is going in: “I think everyone who works in a replaceable field or trade should be planning ahead.”

rows.title: United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby lies on his office floor and takes 20-minute naps—and he says it doesn’t mean he’s accomplished any less
rows.standfirst: Despite taking a quick 20-minute nap on the floor, the United Airlines CEO says he has “accomplished more” than anything else he could have done in that time.

rows.title: Trump’s agricultural tariffs hit all 50 states—driving up food prices, crushing exports, and leaving farmers with nowhere to turn
rows.standfirst: What happens when tariffs hit American agriculture? All 50 states found out.

rows.title: The starter economy is broken
rows.standfirst: Gen Z is entering adulthood to find that jobs, houses, and cars are out of reach—and it’s pushing American optimism to an all-time low.

rows.title: Online response to the attack on Sam Altman’s house shows a generational divide
rows.standfirst: Gen Z is furious about AI, and so is the American countryside.

rows.title: Trump’s economy officially passes Biden’s for worst consumer sentiment in recorded history
rows.standfirst: The University of Michigan’s index plunged to 47.6 in April—shattering the prior floor set during the 2022 inflation crisis.

rows.title: Another month, another record-high home price: March hits $408,800—the 33rd straight increase
rows.standfirst: The median existing home price rose 1.4% from a year ago even as sales fell 3.6%, the NAR reported. Experts say the market needs up to 500,000 more homes to feel normal.

rows.title: Trump’s White House: America is short 10 million houses
rows.standfirst: The White House said regulatory cuts could lead to more construction to stabilize prices, increase home ownership and fuel faster economic growth.

rows.title: The Iran war’s fertilizer shock is hammering American farmers, and 70% can’t afford what they need for this year’s growing season
rows.standfirst: Prices for three main fertilizers used by farmers are all up double digits since the Iran war started.

rows.title: The world’s most — and least — miserable economies in 2025, ranked
rows.standfirst: Venezuela tops a new global misery index covering 178 countries, while Taiwan claims the happiest economy title for the second year running.

rows.title: The CEO of $8.5 billion Japanese car giant Nissan plays the drums in a band and hits the tennis courts to destress from the top job
rows.standfirst: Ivan Espinosa, CEO of Nissan, says playing the drums, tennis, and golf lowers his stress—a tactic quite different from that of Amazon’s Jeff Bezos.

rows.title: The housing crisis has become HR’s problem. Helping workers buy homes near the office is employers’ newest RTO play
rows.standfirst: Workers are saving for retirement but can’t afford to buy a home. Some employers, including BNY, are starting to fill the gap the federal government won’t.

rows.title: Gen Z is carving a different path in the housing market by doing it alone
rows.standfirst: “Gen Zers are absolutely crushing it when we think about singles purchasing homes in this housing market compared to millennials at the same age.”

rows.title: Older millennials are starting to act like boomers in the housing market—and pulling away from the pack
rows.standfirst: The generation once shut out of homeownership is now using equity to trade up, leaving younger buyers further behind.

rows.title: If the economy feels even worse for you than inflation data says, that might be because childcare isn’t deemed a ‘necessity’
rows.standfirst: “The cost of childcare obviously impacts labor force decisions, and that in turn impacts labor growth as a whole,” a BofA economist tells Fortune.

rows.title: Twitter cofounder Jack Dorsey breaks down his thought process when he laid off 40% of his Block staff because of AI
rows.standfirst: Jack Dorsey, CEO of Block, laid off 40% of his staff after working out the “minimal number of people” to run his $41 billion fintech company.

rows.title: Trump’s big housing market solution is dead on arrival, UBS says—its model is Texas from 25 years ago
rows.standfirst: “There isn’t a magic wand that will all of a sudden return housing affordability to its historic average tomorrow,” ResiClub’s Lance Lambert told Fortune.

rows.title: Dana Perino was terrified to leave the White House — until George W. Bush changed how she thinks about her career
rows.standfirst: Former White House press secretary Dana Perino says George W. Bush taught her to stop rigid career planning and focus on now.

rows.title: Zillow’s CEO says his friends were shocked when he quit a cushy Microsoft job—but Steve Jobs led to his success at the $10.5 billion real estate firm
rows.standfirst: Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman left his cushy Microsoft job in 2009 to join the struggling real estate startup during the housing crisis. His friends had concerns—but he turned it around, thanks in part to Steve Jobs.

rows.title: ‘The current system right now is unsustainable’: top economist sees a crucial crack in the economy
rows.standfirst: “The current system right now is unsustainable,” one economist said. As baby boomers age, the problems may only intensify.

rows.title: Parents are so panicked about the job market they’re paying career coaches $15,000 years before their kids graduate from college
rows.standfirst: As the job market grows more brutal for new grads, an industry of high-end career coaches is cashing in on parental anxiety, starting sophomore year.

rows.title: For wealthy buyers, Mar-a-Lago’s security perimeter is Palm Beach’s hottest amenity
rows.standfirst: An indefinite road closure on Billionaires’ Row was supposed to be a hassle. Agents say it’s become a sales pitch.

rows.title: Gen Z is ‘Chinamaxxing’—and it’s less a love letter to Beijing than an indictment of America
rows.standfirst: A viral TikTok trend is handing Beijing a cultural moment that decades of propaganda never could. Are we entering the Chinese century?

rows.title: Nvidia CEO says that AI agents will make workers busier than ever—they’ll ‘harass’ and ‘micromanage’ you, instead of take your job
rows.standfirst: Jensen Huang, CEO of $4.8 trillion tech giant Nvidia, says AI will help humans explore space, get better at their jobs, and live more cost-effectively.

rows.title: This talent CEO says laid-off tech workers are ignoring a $300K ‘white-collar trade job’ with 81K openings a year
rows.standfirst: As AI layoffs threaten the white-collar workforce, the $700 billion data center build-out is minting six-figure technician roles, and employers can’t fill them fast enough.

rows.title: Apple taps John Ternus as its next CEO—and Tim Cook says he is handing down the same advice Steve Jobs gave him
rows.standfirst: Apple insider John Ternus will become CEO of the $4 trillion tech giant this September, and outgoing leader Tim Cook has just revealed the advice he’ll give his successor.

rows.title: Meta will start tracking employees’ screens and keystrokes to train AI tools
rows.standfirst: To build AI workers, tech companies are now mining how humans actually work.

rows.title: The housing affordability crisis isn’t just crushing millennials—it’s squeezing out buyers in their 40s, 50s, and beyond, too
rows.standfirst: “When purchasing power declines, fewer people buy homes at 28—but also fewer purchase at 38 or 48,” writes Housing Center codirector Ed Pinto.

rows.title: The 10 best cities for college grads: Omaha ranks higher than New York and L.A. because Gen Z ‘actually have a shot at purchasing a house’ for under $300K
rows.standfirst: “With a lot of homes selling for under $300,000, young grads actually have a shot at purchasing a house,” one Omaha real estate agent said.

rows.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says you won’t lose your job to AI—you’ll lose it to your coworker who uses it
rows.standfirst: While other tech leaders warn of mass layoffs, Nvidia’s CEO says the real threat is the person sitting next to you.

rows.title: The starter home is dying. Better.com’s CEO says AI is the only thing that can save it
rows.standfirst: Better.com CEO Vishal Garg said AI can service the low mortgages loan officers avoid.

rows.title: Despite nearing their 60s, nearly four in 10 Americans heading towards the end of their careers don’t even have a retirement account
rows.standfirst: Around four in 10 U.S. Gen Xers, and even some baby boomers, haven’t saved for retirement—as current retirees who didn’t save enough endure a “nightmare.”

rows.title: People living in the U.S. with temporary protected status, targeted by Trump, are a $29 billion economic force
rows.standfirst: As the Supreme Court prepares to weigh the fate of TPS for Haitians and Syrians, a new report accounts for a demographic’s economic impact.

rows.title: Ken Griffin’s Citadel fires back at NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani ‘tax the rich’ video featuring his $238 million penthouse
rows.standfirst: Citadel’s COO subtly hinted the company may forgo a potential $6 billion investment in Midtown Manhattan after the NYC Mayor vowed to “tax the rich.”

rows.title: Good news: Rumors of a K-shaped economy are overblown so far, says Goldman Sachs. Bad news: 2026 is the year it will really bite
rows.standfirst: “There are a lot of people out there who can no longer afford perhaps the most quintessential component of the American Dream, which is property ownership. So they’re being forced to rent, and it’s showing up in prices.”

rows.title: Meta executive says he gets stressed only five times a year and that it’s actually ‘a useful signal’
rows.standfirst: Meta chief technology officer Andrew Bosworth says being busy with important matters on the table is his stress “trigger”: He calms down with exercise and deep breathing.

rows.title: Americans are buying more used clothes, but the real story is who’s buying what: Luxury resale is booming and so is discount
rows.standfirst: “We’re seeing that growth isn’t uniform, and it really is concentrated, seemingly, at the high and low ends of the market when it comes to clothes.”

rows.title: With entry-level jobs vanishing, Gen Z grads are ditching corporate America—piecing together careers with entrepreneurship, gig work and freelancing
rows.standfirst: “What we’re seeing now is something less linear, yet their outcomes are actually improving.”

rows.title: I lost my job to AI. Here’s why mass layoffs won’t transform your company
rows.standfirst: Pearl’s Head of AI Operations Mark Quinn was displaced by the same technology he now deploys at scale. That experience taught him the difference between companies that shrink their way to efficiency and the ones that actually reinvent themselves.

rows.title: ‘You feel radicalized’: A Meta AI exec watched agents beat her top workers. Now she’s built a nonprofit to help Gen Z find jobs before they disappear
rows.standfirst: Gen Z is facing AI-driven layoffs and fewer entry-level jobs. Former Meta and Salesforce AI head Clara Shih says young workers can future-proof their careers by learning how to use AI agents.

rows.title: Florida’s influx of rich residents is killing the middle class and housing market
rows.standfirst: The pandemic wave of Florida transplants is backfiring.

rows.title: AI is frying our brains — here’s what leaders need to do about It
rows.standfirst: New research confirms AI isn’t reducing cognitive load — it’s multiplying it. Neuroscience explains what’s causing “brain drain” and offers organizations ways to reverse it.

rows.title: Baby boomers have now ‘gobbled up’ nearly one-third of America’s wealth share, and they’re leaving Gen Z and millennials behind
rows.standfirst: American septuagenarians hold more than $85 trillion in assets—by far the most of any generation.

rows.title: Incoming Apple CEO John Ternus tells Gen Z an early mistake taught him an important lesson: ‘The care you put into your work really matters’
rows.standfirst: John Ternus, the incoming CEO of Apple, advises Gen Z college graduates to pour themselves into work, build skills, and always assume they’re not the smartest in the room.

rows.title: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff says AI won’t kill entry-level jobs. He’s hiring 1,000 new grads to prove it
rows.standfirst: The billionaire said the SaaS giant would hire recent grads to help build its AI platforms.

rows.title: Microsoft researchers have revealed the 40 jobs most exposed to AI—and even teachers make the list
rows.standfirst: Sorry, Gen Z: AI is expected to soon reshape dozens of popular professions—and possibly make some tasks obsolete.

rows.title: CEO of a $25.9 billion bank had his AI clone lead the company’s earnings call—as Mark Zuckerberg builds his own digital twin
rows.standfirst: An AI double of Customers Bank CEO Sam Sidhu led the company’s recent earnings call. He joins Mark Zuckerberg, Sebastian Siemiatkowski, and Eric Yuan in the AI clone trend.

rows.title: U.S. consumer confidence inches up even as the Iran war sends energy prices soaring
rows.standfirst: The Conference Board said Tuesday that its consumer confidence index inched up to 92.8 in April from 92.2 in March.

rows.title: Ray Dalio says the U.S. is ‘certainly in a stagflationary period,’ and what the Fed does next could make or break the economy
rows.standfirst: As affordability crushes consumer confidence to a decades-low, Dalio warns a loss of credibility at the central bank could turn stagflation fears into reality.

rows.title: A 160-year-old paradox explains why AI will create more lawyers and accountants—not fewer, top economist says
rows.standfirst: Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok thinks AI doomers may be proven wrong. Just swap in “people” for “coal” in Jevons Paradox.

rows.title: Meet all 37 White House ballroom donors funding the $400 million build, including Silicon Valley tech giants, crypto bros and the Lutnicks
rows.standfirst: The list, reviewed by Fortune, did not mention specific dollar amounts offered by each contributor.

rows.title: Former Goldman Sachs CEO: Ivy League geniuses aren’t always the most successful—This overlooked skill is key
rows.standfirst: Lloyd Blankfein, the former CEO of Goldman Sachs, said that his career “is not only relatable, but accessible”—it requires work ethic and a keen eye for opportunities.

rows.title: ‘They left me no choice’: Powell isn’t going anywhere—blocking Trump from another Fed appointee
rows.standfirst: Powell said he’ll step down when the DOJ’s investigation is “well and truly over,” with no threats of revival.

rows.title: Hilton’s CEO says the economy is actually C-shaped to the benefit of the middle class. Most of his competitors disagree
rows.standfirst: Hilton is the contrarian in a travel and hospitality sector that has been leaning into luxury as its primary growth engine.

rows.title: The global economy has a month—eight weeks at most—to avoid a recession, warns top economist
rows.standfirst: “The irony in all this is that the U.S., which started the war, does better in relative terms than anybody else because of its energy supplies.”

rows.title: The biggest jump in 3 years: gas’ effect on core inflation in March revealed
rows.standfirst: The jump in gas prices has pushed inflation further away from the Fed’s 2% target.

rows.title: Your laundry bill is about to get more expensive—and Unilever says the Iran war is partly to blame
rows.standfirst: “There will be frequent price increases, but in small doses,” Unilever CFO Srinivas Phatak told analysts on Thursday.
